new_statements.quote: In Iyive tone is contrastive at both the lexical and grammatical level. [p. 23] … Mono-syllabic words can have one of the following patterns: L, H, HL, LH. [p. 24] … The definition of a phonological syllable in Iyive is that it has a vowel nucleus and carries contrastive tone. [p. 21] … Vowel length is conditioned by tone. The only time long vowels are heard is where there is a contour tone. [p. 18]
new_statements.citation: Foster, Suzanne E. 2012. A Phonology Sketch of the Iyive Language. Yaounde: SIL (Ministry of Scientific Research and Innovation). SIL Language & Culture Archives 52746.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened and page images of Foster 2012, printed pp. 23-24) and viewed them directly, plus the scanned file for PDF pages 019, 022, 023, 026, 033 and the intro (005). All four quoted sentences are present verbatim at the stated locators: "In Iyive tone is contrastive at both the lexical and grammatical level." (p. 23, section 5 Tone, first sentence, seen in the image); "Mono-syllabic words can have one of the following patterns: L, H, HL, LH." (p. 24, seen in the image); "The definition of a phonological syllable in Iyive is that it has a vowel nucleus and carries contrastive tone." (p. 21, section 4, scanned); "Vowel length is conditioned by tone. The only time long vowels are heard is where…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for word stress is given. The only prosodic description is tonal: two level tones (H, L) plus falling and rising contours, contrastive lexically (e.g. /ìhɔ́/ 'knife' vs /íhɔ́/ 'day') and grammatically (tense, 2nd vs 3rd person, singular/plural in one noun class, a final HL question clitic); tone melodies are listed for mono-, di- and trisyllabic words. Stress, accent or prominence is never mentioned in the 92-page sketch.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress (none discussed). Tone analysis is explicitly preliminary ('There has not been sufficient time to do in-depth analysis at the tone level', p. 23); downstep flagged for further study (p. 32).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone patterns on citation forms (verbs, nouns with class prefix) plus phrase-level tonal effects (question clitic); no word-stress domain statement exists.
new_statements.identity_note: Foster 2012 describes 'the Iyive language' [uiv] = Glottolog iyiv1238 (Blench atlas aliases Uive, Yiive, Ndir; Cameroon cover term Asumbo). Data were gathered in Manko village (Assumbo/Ipulo territory, Cameroon) from a displaced Yive family and a 1700-word list (main informant Pastor David Iwen Menge); no dialect is distinguished. Ethnologue (cited by Foster) gives 75% lexical similarity with Tiv.

sources.note: Nothing. The whole sketch (consonants, vowels, long vowels, vowel harmony, syllable structure, §5 Tone pp. 23-25, plural formation, morphophonemics, conclusion, 1700-item word list, alphabet chart) never uses the words stress, accent, prominence or intonation (scanned grep of all 92 pages: only 'distress' in a gloss). Prosody is described only as tone: 'In Iyive tone is contrastive at both the lexical and grammatical level' (p. 23); tone patterns L, H, HL, LH for monosyllables and lists of di-/trisyllabic tone melodies (p. 24); vowel length conditioned by contour tone (p. 18); syllable define…

sources.citation: Blench, Roger. 2016. New research on Tivoid and its place within Bantoid. Paper/slides, Bantu 6, Helsinki, 22 June 2016.
sources.note: Comparative. Says modern phonologies exist for only five Tivoid languages (Tiv, Iyive, Iceve, Esimbi, Ugarə); illustrates Iyive plural formation including 'tonal alternation'; no word on stress/accent for any Tivoid language.

sources.citation: Blench, Roger. 2024. An overview of the Bantoid languages. Afrika und Übersee 97. DOI 10.15460/auue.2024.97.1.288
sources.note: Comparative survey. Cites Foster (2012) only in Table 5 (ATR vowel harmony present in Iyive) and lists 'Foster, Suzanne E. 2012. A phonology sketch of the Iyive language. ms.'; §4.2.6 on tones does not mention Iyive; nothing on stress.
